A call to eliminate windfall taxes and halt reserve releases claims it will fix high gas prices.
Evidence: Free market supply, Sustained consumer burden, Producer margin protection
#Aletheia #EnergyPolicy

Advocates argue that letting oil prices soar without government intervention or reserve releases will incentivize drillers to rapidly boost domestic production and restore market equilibrium.
Stated Judgement: (+0.68, +0.42) — Lesser Good

Removing regulatory oversight and consumer protections locks in record energy inflation, allowing oil producers to extract maximum margins while transferring the full burden of supply shocks onto the public.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.74, -0.71) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception. The proposal conflates upstream corporate margin defense with long-term consumer affordability.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 14.20, Uncertainty z: 4)

- Upstream Energy Lobby: FAIL (-0.78, -0.75) — Shifts inflation risk to public.

The Federalist published an op-ed arguing that the federal government must stop releasing emergency reserves, ditch windfall profit taxes, and allow higher retail prices to stimulate drilling.

The Bright Side:
High market prices can naturally signal exploration capital, provided producers reinvest profits into new capacity rather than purely returning cash via stock buybacks.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The analysis confuses producer incentive (WHAT) with public welfare (WHO). It treats unrestrained price spikes as a cure rather than an acute economic strain on households.

Social Physics Analysis:
The proposal executes a classic Smart Selfish maneuver. Actors manufacture a policy pretext—blaming emergency price dampening for drilling hesitance—to insulate windfall producer margins while projecting systemic supply failures onto public stabilization measures.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil, shifting structural energy volatility directly onto working-class consumers.

The Unavoidable Truth: High oil prices enrich drilling operators long before new supply reaches the pump.
The Unavoidable Lie: Removing consumer price protections instantly solves structural global supply shortages.

Alethekanon:
Treating runaway retail prices as a policy virtue ignores the real-world friction of capital discipline and refining caps.

Awwthekanon:
Working families cannot simply absorb record fuel costs while waiting for speculative drilling promises to materialize.

Brothekanon:
Telling drivers to just pay more at the pump so oil executives feel confident enough to drill is a wild sales pitch.

Spirithekanon:
"He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it." Proverbs 11:26 FAIL
Exploiting essential resource scarcity for speculative gain subverts moral stewardship of the common good.

Five Things America Must Do To Rein In Oil Prices

Stop talking the price down, take the windfall profits tax off the table, quit using the reserve as a price tool, and more.

Actual Article Body:
Stop talking the price down, take the windfall profits tax off the table, quit using the reserve as a price tool, and more.

Since the United States went to war with Iran in late February, the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed, the Red Sea route has come under fire, and on Sept. 10 drones knocked out the Saudi pipeline that carried millions of barrels a day around Hormuz. Retail diesel just set an all-time record. Washington has spent seven months managing the price instead of the shortage: the largest coordinated reserve release in history, shipping-law waivers, a peace memorandum that didn’t hold, and public pressure on producers to cut what they charge. Each move took the price down for a few days. None of them added an additional barrel to the market. Along the way we starved the one mechanism that reliably ends a shortage: increasing supply.

That mechanism isn’t complicated. Supply gets tight. Prices rise. Higher prices make marginal wells economic, so capital commits to drilling programs, programs put rigs to work, and barrels arrive. The new supply pushes prices back down on its own, and the country restocks along the way. No governmental authority administers that. Thousands of drilling operators decide independently whether the number works, and that has bailed this country out of every supply shock in my lifetime. This year, this mechanism has barely been allowed to run.

Look at what should be the strongest signal in a generation: American refineries have run near 97 percent of capacity for more than a month. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve sits at 285 million barrels, the lowest since 1982, back when we were still filling it. Add it to commercial stocks and the country holds less crude than at any point in the weekly record going back to 1990. That is a screaming shortage.

Now look at the response. Over the past year, the country has added 34 oil rigs. Thirty-four, against a war, a closed strait, and the thinnest crude position on record. People outside this business read that as greed or timidity. In reality, drilling operators are hesitating to add more oil rigs because they question whether the price will last long enough to justify the commitment.

Nobody drills one well. An operator commits a program: rig contracts, completion crews, takeaway capacity and permits, ramped up over quarters and running well past the payback on any single well.

Until this month, every rally was talked down inside a news cycle. A statement from the White House about a deal with Iran that then fell through. A release from a strategic oil reserve we could no longer afford to draw. A president telling the largest producers they “ought to give some of that [profit] back” to consumers. The barrels behind Hormuz didn’t move because somebody posted something. What actually happened is that the market signal died before any capital could commit to it, and the thing that would have fixed the shortage never got funded by public and private industry.

September has been a test of the alternative. Brent crude, an oil pricing indicator, broke above $100 when the Saudi pipeline went down, for the first time since May. The rig count has risen two weeks running to its highest since May 2024. It’s the first stretch all year where operators are acting like they believe the price. It will stop the moment Washington decides the price is its problem to fix.

Meanwhile the books are balancing a different way. Commercial crude inventories sit right at their five-year average, largely because 130 million barrels have come out of the emergency reserve since February. We moved oil from the savings account to the checking account and called it stability. The rest is coming out of consumption. Retail diesel hit $6.29 a gallon last week, the highest since the government began tracking it in 1994 and up about 65 percent since the war began, while diesel demand is running 3.3 percent below a year ago.
